summary.title: Pablo Bessone
summary.description: Building web applications professionally since 2020 with React, TypeScript, Node.js and NestJS. My experience includes AngularJS modernization, microfrontends, REST APIs and ERP integrations.

about.text1: I'm a full stack developer with a frontend focus. Since 2020, I've worked on web interfaces, backend services and business integrations. I enjoy frontend architecture and UI work, and I'm equally willing to work on APIs, databases and end-to-end features.
about.text2: At We Are Psh, I work with React, Redux and TypeScript, modernize AngularJS screens, and contribute to microfrontends and a shared component library. On the backend, I develop and maintain NestJS services and REST APIs connected to MySQL, alongside Docker and CI/CD workflows.
about.text3: Previously, at Futit Services, I integrated Jira and Scaleway with Openbravo/Etendo and developed WebPOS interfaces. That work involved databases, business workflows and direct client support.
about.text4: My personal projects explore local-first applications, browser-based databases, optional cloud synchronization and automated testing. Their case studies explain the implementation choices and current limitations, not just the technology stack.

Implement and maintain React/TypeScript microfrontends and contribute to the team's shared component library.
Develop and maintain REST APIs and TypeScript/NestJS microservices connected to MySQL for user-status information.
Integrate frontend and backend user events with Mixpanel for product analytics.
Configure and maintain CI/CD pipelines for microfrontends and microservices, and troubleshoot Docker containers.
pshHighlights: Contribute to both legacy modernization and shared frontend infrastructure, rather than only building isolated screens.
Apply team coding conventions across UI and service work to keep implementations consistent and maintainable.
futitResponsibilities: Integrated Jira with the ERP to synchronize tasks, statuses and worklogs used by the management team.
Integrated Scaleway with Openbravo/Etendo so server creation could be managed from the ERP.
Developed frontend functionality for Openbravo WebPOS, working on e-commerce interfaces and user flows.
Managed databases and provided direct client support for business application workflows.
futitHighlights: Connected external services to existing ERP workflows, bringing task tracking and server management into the tools the team already used.
Combined frontend development with integration work and direct contact with clients.

problem: Take and organize rich-text notes without requiring an account, while offering cloud synchronization for users who sign in.
architecture: React and TypeScript handle the interface, TipTap handles rich-text editing, and repository adapters separate note and folder operations from localStorage and Firestore persistence.
Local data is migrated when a user first signs in. The migration compares edit timestamps, processes writes in batches and tracks migrated records.
decisions: Local-first storage keeps account creation optional. Supporting both local and remote data adds migration and reconciliation responsibilities that a cloud-only CRUD interface would avoid.
Migration waits for queued edits and recalculates pending changes before committing. Newer edits take precedence; this is timestamp-based reconciliation, not collaborative text merging.
quality: Vitest tests cover data-layer behavior. Firebase emulator tests exercise security rules, user isolation and repository integration. Playwright covers offline-only browser workflows.

The repository's CI workflow is configured to run lint, formatting checks, build, unit tests, Firebase tests and E2E tests. Cloud-sync behavior is not comprehensively covered by the offline E2E suite.
limitations: Local-only notes depend on browser storage. Cloud synchronization requires an account and connectivity, and failures still need to be handled explicitly.
Timestamp-based reconciliation does not preserve both versions of every conflicting edit. This project does not claim lossless collaborative editing or guaranteed recovery from every network failure.

problem: Manage monthly income, recurring expenses and daily spending without accounts or a remote database. Keep the financial data in a password-protected file controlled by the user.
architecture: React calls a typed worker protocol rather than issuing SQL from components. A Web Worker runs sql.js/SQLite in memory, with domain repositories, transactions and versioned migrations.
The database is exported into a versioned .nimvo container using Web Crypto: AES-256-GCM and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256. Financial data is not stored in localStorage; presentation preferences are.
decisions: Amounts use integer cents instead of floating-point arithmetic. Marking a fixed expense as paid changes its pending status, not the balance, because the amount was already reserved.

A local file removes the need for a hosted financial-data service, but makes saving, backups and password custody the user's responsibility. Supported Chromium browsers can write to a chosen file; other browsers can download a copy.
quality: Vitest and React Testing Library cover money calculations, repositories, migrations, encrypted containers and component behavior. Playwright suites cover Chromium and Firefox flows, file handling, keyboard navigation and basic accessibility checks.
The tests include altered or truncated files and incorrect passwords, not only successful encryption and decryption. Automated checks do not constitute an independent security audit.
limitations: No built-in synchronization, collaboration or password recovery. Unsaved changes can be lost, and parallel edits to separate file copies are not reconciled.
A fully loaded tab can operate without a network connection, but there is no service worker or PWA cache: opening or reloading the app still requires the host to be available.

problem: Build a Tetris-style browser game with timed chaos effects, softcore and hardcore modes, and local rankings that can work independently of the online leaderboard.
architecture: A React interface surrounds the Excalibur.js/TypeScript game engine. Chaos effects are selected from a pool unlocked by the current level.
Global rankings use Supabase anonymous authentication, Edge Functions to create and submit runs, and PostgreSQL for storage and ranking queries. Local history stays separate from online submissions.
decisions: Prepare an online run before gameplay instead of uploading arbitrary local history afterward. Validate submissions server-side and use request limits and idempotency to reduce abuse and duplicate submissions.
Keep local play available when online services are disabled or fail. Rankings are separated by mode so different rulesets are not mixed.
quality: Node regression tests exercise ranking limits, storage failures, disabled-online behavior, guest CAPTCHA handling and offline fallback.
The repository also provides PostgreSQL tests, Edge Function type checking, lint and build commands. These are separate checks for the browser, service boundary and database.
limitations: Scores are calculated by the client. Server validation and rate limits reduce abuse but do not make the leaderboard an authoritative or cheat-proof competitive system.
Online publishing requires connectivity and a run prepared before the game. Existing local scores are not uploaded retroactively. This is not an opponent-to-opponent multiplayer game.

problem: Present professional experience and engineering projects in English and Spanish, with content that is available immediately and navigable without JavaScript.
architecture: Astro owns document metadata, localized routes and build output. React sections render at build time without hydrated islands; SCSS Modules share design tokens.
A project catalog supplies cards, localized case-study routes and sitemap entries. A small browser script enhances the mobile menu, language links and scroll controls.
decisions: Static rendering keeps the content independent of client-side React startup. The existing root URL remains available and points canonically to the English version.
Language selection links to the equivalent localized page. Existing project URLs remain available even when they are no longer featured on the homepage.
quality: Vitest tests cover menu behavior, Escape handling, scroll thresholds, reduced motion and language-link fragments.
Generated-HTML checks inspect localized content, canonical and alternate URLs, images, internal links, CV download, case studies, sitemap entries and the absence of hydrated React islands.
limitations: Content updates require a rebuild. There is no CMS or contact-form backend; contact is through email and professional profile links.
Project descriptions and test configurations are documented in the source repositories. This site does not provide live test-run reports or usage analytics.

problem: Provide a small, playful interface for finding the next day of the week.
architecture: React and TypeScript provide the interface, with Chakra UI components and a Vite build.
decisions: Keep the interaction narrow and easy to understand. This smaller UI project is retained as an additional example, rather than the main evidence of full stack engineering.
quality: The source repository is available for reviewing the interface and day-calculation implementation. This case study does not claim automated test coverage.
limitations: A deliberately small frontend-only application: it does not demonstrate backend services, persistence or distributed-system behavior.
